why_use_this:
Reach for this package the moment a computation needs \( i = \sqrt{-1} \) -- roots of a negative discriminant, AC circuit analysis, Fourier/frequency-domain work (see [vani-signal](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-signal), which depends on this package for exactly that), or anywhere a real-only type like `f64` simply can't represent the answer. `Complex` is a plain `{ re: f64, im: f64 }` struct with no heap-owning fields, so it's freely copyable -- every function here takes and returns `Complex` by value, no `ref`/`mut ref` ceremony anywhere, unlike the `Vec<f64>`-based sibling libraries. If your problem never leaves the reals (no square roots of negative numbers, no oscillating phase/frequency content), you don't need this package at all -- reach for it specifically when a real number stops being enough.

A running example, \(z_1=3+4i\), threads through the arithmetic/polar notes below -- deliberately a 3-4-5 triangle so \(|z_1|=5\) comes out clean.

complex_conj.intuition: Flip the sign of the imaginary part only -- geometrically, this reflects the point across the real (horizontal) axis in the complex plane.
complex_conj.why: Conjugation is the trick behind `complex_div`/`complex_reciprocal`'s whole approach: multiplying \(z\) by \(\bar{z}\) always produces a REAL number (\(a^2+b^2\)), which is what lets you clear the imaginary part out of a denominator.

complex_neg.intuition: Flip the sign of BOTH parts -- geometrically, rotates the point 180° through the origin.
complex_neg.why: Unlike `complex_conj` (which only flips the imaginary part, reflecting across the horizontal axis), negation flips BOTH, reflecting through the origin entirely -- two visually different operations that are easy to confuse by name alone.

complex_add.intuition: Add real parts together and imaginary parts together, completely independently -- geometrically, this is exactly vector addition: place one arrow at the tip of the other and see where you land.
complex_add.why: Complex addition behaving exactly like 2D vector addition is why complex numbers are such a natural fit for anything already thought of as a 2D vector (AC circuit phasors, 2D rotations) -- the arithmetic you already know from vectors carries over directly.

complex_sub.intuition: Same as `complex_add`, with subtraction in each component.
complex_sub.why: Geometrically, \(z_1-z_2\) is the vector pointing FROM \(z_2\) TO \(z_1\) -- useful for finding the direction and distance between two points in the complex plane, the same way vector subtraction works for ordinary 2D points.

complex_mul.intuition: Multiply the two complex numbers out like two binomials (FOIL), then simplify using the one special rule of complex arithmetic: \(i^2=-1\).
complex_mul.example: \((3+4i)(1+2i) = 3\times1 + 3\times2i + 4i\times1 + 4i\times2i = 3+6i+4i+8i^2 = 3+10i-8 = -5+10i\) (using \(i^2=-1\) on the last term). Matches the formula directly: \((3\times1-4\times2)+(3\times2+4\times1)i = (3-8)+(6+4)i=-5+10i\).
complex_mul.why: Geometrically, multiplying complex numbers MULTIPLIES their magnitudes and ADDS their angles -- a fact that isn't obvious from this Cartesian formula at all, but becomes clear once you look at multiplication in polar form (see `complex_from_polar`).

complex_norm_sq.intuition: The squared distance from the origin -- cheaper to compute than the true distance (`complex_abs`) because it skips the square root, useful whenever you only need to COMPARE magnitudes or use one as a denominator.
complex_norm_sq.why: This is exactly the \(25\) that shows up as the denominator in `complex_div`'s and `complex_reciprocal`'s worked examples below -- both are built directly on top of this function.

complex_div.intuition: You can't directly "divide" by a complex number the way you divide by a real one -- the standard trick is to multiply both the numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate, which turns the denominator into a plain real number (via `complex_norm_sq`) that ordinary division handles fine.
complex_div.example: \(\dfrac{3+4i}{1+2i}\): multiply top and bottom by \(1-2i\): numerator \((3+4i)(1-2i) = 3-6i+4i-8i^2 = 3-2i+8=11-2i\); denominator \(1^2+2^2=5\). Result: \(\dfrac{11-2i}{5} = 2.2-0.4i\).
complex_div.why: This same conjugate-multiplication trick is exactly what `complex_reciprocal` does as the special case \(1/z\) (i.e. \(a=1,b=0\)) -- `complex_div` is the more general form.

complex_scale.intuition: Multiplying by a plain real number stretches (or shrinks, or flips if negative) the complex number without rotating it at all -- both parts scale by the same factor.
complex_scale.why: Because this is the \(n=1\)-dimensional special case of `complex_mul` where the second operand has zero imaginary part, scaling never rotates the result -- multiplying by a genuinely complex number (nonzero imaginary part) is what introduces rotation, as `complex_mul`'s own note explains.

complex_reciprocal.intuition: The same conjugate-over-norm-squared trick as `complex_div`, specialized to "1 divided by" a single complex number.
complex_reciprocal.why: Sanity check: multiply the original \(z_1=3+4i\) by this reciprocal and you should get back \(1\) -- \((3+4i)(0.12-0.16i) = (3\times0.12 - 4\times(-0.16)) + (\ldots)i = (0.36+0.64)+0i = 1.0+0i\), confirming this really is \(1/z_1\).

complex_abs.intuition: The straight-line distance from the origin to the point \((a,b)\) -- ordinary Pythagorean distance, since the complex plane IS just the ordinary 2D plane with a name for each axis.
complex_abs.example: \(|3+4i| = \sqrt{9+16} = \sqrt{25}=5\) -- the same 3-4-5 right triangle this running example was chosen for.
complex_abs.why: This is the \(r\) in \(z\)'s polar form \(re^{i\theta}\) (see `complex_from_polar`) -- every complex number is uniquely described by how FAR it is from the origin (this) and which DIRECTION it points (`complex_arg`).

complex_arg.intuition: The angle (measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis) that the point \((a,b)\) sits at -- the same angle you'd read off a compass if the positive real axis pointed "east".
complex_arg.example: \(\arg(3+4i) = \operatorname{atan2}(4,3) \approx 0.9273\) radians (about \(53.13°\)) -- the angle of a 3-4-5 right triangle's non-right angle opposite the side of length 4.
complex_arg.why: Using \(\operatorname{atan2}\) rather than plain \(\arctan(b/a)\) is essential: plain arctan can't tell \((3,4)\) apart from \((-3,-4)\) (both give the same \(b/a\) ratio), but they point in completely opposite directions -- `atan2` uses BOTH signs to place the angle in the correct quadrant.

complex_from_polar.intuition: The reverse of the (`complex_abs`, `complex_arg`) pair: given a distance and a direction, place the point.
complex_from_polar.example: Using \(r=5\), \(\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(4,3)\approx0.9273\) (from \(z_1=3+4i\)'s own polar form): \(5\cos(0.9273)\approx5\times0.6=3\) and \(5\sin(0.9273)\approx5\times0.8=4\), recovering \((3,4)\), i.e. \(z_1\) itself.
complex_from_polar.why: Round-tripping through `complex_abs`/`complex_arg` and back through `complex_from_polar` is a useful sanity check that these three functions agree with each other -- and this Cartesian-to-polar-and-back conversion is exactly what `complex_sqrt` uses internally to take a square root.

complex_exp.intuition: A complex exponential doesn't grow explosively the way a real exponential can -- Euler's formula reveals that the imaginary part of the exponent only ever ROTATES, while the real part of the exponent controls SCALING. So \(e^{a+bi}\) is "scale by \(e^a\), then rotate by \(b\) radians."
complex_exp.example: The single most famous instance: \(z=i\pi\) (\(a=0,b=\pi\)). \(e^{i\pi} = e^0(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi) = 1\times(-1+0i) = -1\) -- Euler's identity, \(e^{i\pi}=-1\), or as it's often written, \(e^{i\pi}+1=0\), tying together five of the most fundamental constants in mathematics in one equation.
complex_exp.why: Because the real part of the exponent (\(a\)) controls scaling completely SEPARATELY from how the imaginary part (\(b\)) controls rotation, a purely imaginary exponent (\(a=0\), as in \(e^{i\pi}\)) always lands EXACTLY on the unit circle (magnitude 1) -- it can rotate to any angle, but it never scales at all.

complex_log.intuition: The inverse of `complex_exp`, restricted to one consistent choice of angle (since adding any multiple of \(2\pi\) to an angle gives the same point back, the complex logarithm is technically multi-valued -- this function picks the PRINCIPAL branch, matching `complex_arg`'s own \((-\pi,\pi]\) range).
complex_log.why: Because this is restricted to the principal branch, `complex_exp(complex_log(z))` always recovers \(z\) exactly, but `complex_log(complex_exp(z))` does NOT always recover the original \(z\) -- only when \(z\)'s imaginary part already lies within \((-\pi,\pi]\). This asymmetry is a direct, unavoidable consequence of the logarithm being multi-valued in general and this function picking just one branch.

complex_pow_i64.intuition: Raising to an integer power is just repeated multiplication (or repeated reciprocal-then-multiplication for a negative exponent) -- no special formula needed beyond `complex_mul` itself, applied several times.
complex_pow_i64.formula: \(z^n\) via repeated `complex_mul` (or `complex_reciprocal` of \(z^{|n|}\) for negative \(n\)) -- not De Moivre's polar formula, though the two always agree.
complex_pow_i64.why: This result, \(-7+24i\), reappears directly in `complex_sqrt`'s worked example below -- taking the square root of \(-7+24i\) should recover \(3+4i\), the number we just squared to get there, a nice built-in consistency check between the two functions.

complex_sqrt.intuition: There's no simple Cartesian formula for a complex square root, but polar form makes it easy: halve the angle and take the square root of the distance -- since squaring in polar form DOUBLES the angle and squares the distance, halving/rooting is exactly the inverse operation.
complex_sqrt.example: Take the square root of \(-7+24i\) -- exactly `complex_pow_i64`'s result for \((3+4i)^2\) above, so we already know the answer should be \(3+4i\) (or its negation). \(|-7+24i| = \sqrt{49+576}=\sqrt{625}=25\), so \(\sqrt{r}=\sqrt{25}=5\). Halving the angle and converting back via `complex_from_polar` with radius \(5\) lands back on \((3,4)\), i.e. \(3+4i\) -- confirmed algebraically by simply checking \((3+4i)^2=-7+24i\) directly, which `complex_pow_i64`'s example already verified.
complex_sqrt.why: There are always TWO square roots of any nonzero complex number (here, \(3+4i\) and its negation \(-3-4i\), since both square to the same value) -- this function returns the PRINCIPAL one specifically, the one with non-negative real part, resolving the ambiguity by convention rather than returning both.

complex_sin.intuition: Unlike the real sine (always trapped between \(-1\) and \(1\)), the complex sine can grow arbitrarily large -- because it's built from `sinh`/`cosh`, which grow WITHOUT bound, in the imaginary direction.
complex_sin.example: Take a PURELY IMAGINARY input, \(z=2i\) (so \(a=0,b=2\)): \(\sin(2i) = \sin(0)\cosh(2) + i\cos(0)\sinh(2) = 0 + i\times1\times\sinh(2) = i\sinh(2) \approx 3.627i\) -- a value with magnitude well OVER \(1\), something the real sine could never produce.
complex_sin.why: This unboundedness is a genuine, important difference from real trigonometry -- code written assuming \(|\sin(z)|\le1\) (a safe assumption for real \(z\)) would silently give wrong results if \(z\) ever has a nonzero imaginary part.

complex_cos.intuition: Same unbounded-via-cosh/sinh structure as `complex_sin`, for cosine.
complex_cos.example: At \(z=2i\) (\(a=0,b=2\)): \(\cos(2i) = \cos(0)\cosh(2) - i\sin(0)\sinh(2) = 1\times\cosh(2) - 0 = \cosh(2) \approx 3.762\) -- purely REAL (no imaginary part at all, since \(\sin(0)=0\) kills that term), but with magnitude well over \(1\), again something impossible for the real cosine.
complex_cos.why: Notice \(\cos(2i)\) came out purely real while `complex_sin`'s \(\sin(2i)\) came out purely imaginary -- a nice illustration of the identity \(\cos(bi)=\cosh(b)\) and \(\sin(bi)=i\sinh(b)\) for purely imaginary inputs, a special case worth remembering.

complex_tan.intuition: No separate formula needed -- tangent is just sine divided by cosine, computed from values these two functions already know how to produce.
complex_tan.example: At \(z=2i\): \(\tan(2i) = \sin(2i)/\cos(2i) = i\sinh(2)/\cosh(2) = i\tanh(2) \approx 0.964i\) (reusing `complex_sin`'s and `complex_cos`'s results at the same point).
complex_tan.why: Because this is built directly from `complex_sin`/`complex_cos` via `complex_div`, it inherits `complex_div`'s one caveat for free: it's undefined wherever \(\cos z=0\), the complex generalization of the real tangent's familiar vertical asymptotes.

complex_sinh.intuition: The hyperbolic sine's complex generalization -- structurally the mirror image of `complex_sin`'s formula, with `sin`/`cos` and `sinh`/`cosh` swapping roles.
complex_sinh.example: At \(z=2i\) (\(a=0,b=2\)): \(\sinh(2i) = \sinh(0)\cos(2) + i\cosh(0)\sin(2) = 0 + i\times1\times\sin(2) \approx 0.909i\) -- purely imaginary, and this time BOUNDED (since it's built from the ordinary, bounded real sine, not sinh).
complex_sinh.why: Compare directly with `complex_sin(2i)\approx3.627i` -- `complex_sinh` at a purely imaginary input stays modest while `complex_sin` at the same input grows large, the exact opposite of their usual real-axis behavior, because swapping which trig identity leads and which follows swaps which one inherits the unbounded growth.

complex_cosh.intuition: Same swapped-roles structure as `complex_sinh`, for hyperbolic cosine.
complex_cosh.example: At \(z=2i\): \(\cosh(2i) = \cosh(0)\cos(2) + i\sinh(0)\sin(2) = 1\times\cos(2) + 0 \approx -0.416\) -- purely real, and bounded like an ordinary cosine, since \(\cos(2)\) itself is always in \([-1,1]\).
complex_cosh.why: This identity, \(\cosh(bi)=\cos(b)\), is exactly why hyperbolic and ordinary trigonometric functions are often described as "the same functions, rotated 90° into the complex plane" -- evaluating `complex_cosh` at a purely imaginary input literally IS evaluating the real cosine.

complex_tanh.intuition: Same ratio idea as `complex_tan`, for the hyperbolic functions.
complex_tanh.example: At \(z=2i\): \(\tanh(2i) = \sinh(2i)/\cosh(2i) = i\sin(2)/\cos(2) = i\tan(2) \approx -2.185i\) (using `complex_sinh`'s and `complex_cosh`'s results at the same point, and noting \(\tan(2)\) is negative since 2 radians is past \(\pi/2\)).
complex_tanh.why: Built from `complex_sinh`/`complex_cosh` via `complex_div`, exactly mirroring how `complex_tan` is built from `complex_sin`/`complex_cos` -- the same composition pattern applied to the hyperbolic side.

complex_nth_roots_of_unity.intuition: The solutions to \(z^n=1\) are always \(n\) points spaced EQUALLY around the unit circle -- picture a clock face with \(n\) evenly-spaced marks instead of 12.
complex_nth_roots_of_unity.example: For \(n=4\): \(z_0=e^0=1\). \(z_1=e^{i\pi/2}=\cos(90°)+i\sin(90°)=i\). \(z_2=e^{i\pi}=-1\) (Euler's identity again, from `complex_exp`'s example, at exactly this angle). \(z_3=e^{i3\pi/2}=-i\). So the four 4th roots of unity are \(\{1,\,i,\,-1,\,-i\}\) -- the four "compass points" of the unit circle, each 90° apart. Check: \(i^4=(i^2)^2=(-1)^2=1\), confirming \(i\) really is a 4th root of unity.
complex_nth_roots_of_unity.why: These roots always come in this evenly-spaced pattern regardless of \(n\) -- doubling \(n\) to 8 would give 8 points 45° apart instead, always covering the full circle exactly once, which is why they're called roots of UNITY (they all satisfy \(z^n=1\)) and why they show up constantly in signal processing (the FFT's "twiddle factors", see [vani-signal](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-signal), are built from exactly these points).
